questions.stem: How many grammatical genders do German nouns have?
questions.explanation: Masculine, feminine and neuter — der, die and das. French has two, so a student coming from French has an extra one to track, and it cannot be worked out from the meaning.

questions.stem: What is unusual about every German noun in writing?
options: It starts with a capital letter
questions.explanation: Every noun is capitalised, anywhere in a sentence — „das Buch“, „die Schule“, „der Hund“. It makes nouns easy to spot when reading, which is genuinely useful for a beginner.

questions.stem: Which article goes with a neuter singular noun?
questions.explanation: „Das“ is neuter, „der“ masculine and „die“ feminine. „Den“ is not a gender at all — it is the masculine article in the accusative case.

questions.stem: What is the plural definite article in German?
questions.explanation: „Die“ covers every gender in the plural, which is one thing German makes easier. It is also the feminine singular, so the article alone does not tell you whether something is plural.

questions.stem: Where does the verb go in a normal German statement?
questions.explanation: The verb takes the second position, whatever comes first. „Heute spiele ich Fußball“ puts „heute“ first, so the verb still comes second and the subject moves after it.

questions.stem: What does „ich“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Ich“ is I. The set worth learning in order is ich, du, er/sie/es, wir, ihr, sie/Sie — verb endings are taught against that sequence.

questions.stem: What is the difference between „du“ and „Sie“?
options: „Du“ is used in writing and „Sie“ only in speech
„Du“ is informal; „Sie“ is formal and always capitalised
„Du“ is singular and „Sie“ is always plural
„Du“ is present tense and „Sie“ is past
questions.explanation: „Sie“ meaning 'you' keeps its capital letter wherever it appears, which is how it is told apart from „sie“ meaning she or they. When unsure with an adult, „Sie“ is the safe choice.

questions.stem: How do you make a German sentence negative?
questions.explanation: „Ich verstehe nicht“ — the „nicht“ follows. English puts 'not' before the main verb, which is the habit to break. „Nein“ is the answer to a question, not a way to negate a sentence.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich ___ Deutsch“ (to speak)?
questions.explanation: The „ich“ ending is -e. „Sprechen“ is a stem-changing verb, so „du sprichst“ and „er spricht“ change the vowel — but the „ich“ form keeps the original stem.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Wir ___ nach Hause“ (to go)?
questions.explanation: The „wir“ ending is -en, which is identical to the infinitive. That coincidence makes „wir“ one of the easier forms to get right.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Du ___ einen Hund“ (to have)?
questions.explanation: „Haben“ is irregular: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben. The „du“ form drops the b, which is the part most often written wrong.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er ___ Deutscher“ (to be)?
questions.explanation: „Sein“ is the most irregular verb in German: ich bin, du bist, er ist, wir sind. It has to be memorised outright.

questions.stem: In „Ich sehe den Hund“, why is it „den“ and not „der“?
options: The sentence is in the past tense
The dog is the direct object, so it takes the accusative
questions.explanation: German marks the object by changing the article rather than the word order. Masculine „der“ becomes „den“ in the accusative — and masculine is the only gender that visibly changes.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going to the cinema today'?
questions.explanation: Starting with „heute“ pushes the subject after the verb, because the verb must stay in second position. Keeping English order gives „heute ich gehe“, which is the classic beginner error.

questions.stem: Which is the correct plural of „das Buch“?
questions.explanation: German plurals are irregular and this one adds an umlaut and -er. Every plural is worth learning with the word, because no rule predicts them reliably.

questions.stem: What does „Es gibt“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Es gibt“ is fixed and does not change for plural. Translating it word for word gives 'it gives', which is how the phrase is built but not what it means.

questions.stem: Which possessive means 'my' before a masculine noun in the nominative?
questions.explanation: „Mein Bruder“, but „meine Schwester“ for feminine. The possessive takes the same endings as „ein“, which is why they are taught together.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I do not have a dog'?
questions.explanation: German negates a noun with „kein“ rather than „nicht ein“. „Hund“ is masculine and the object, so it takes the accusative „keinen“.

questions.stem: Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: With a modal verb, the second verb goes to the very end of the clause as an infinitive. English keeps them together — 'I would like to eat an apple' — and that habit is what the wrong options show.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'because I am tired'?
questions.explanation: „Weil“ sends the verb to the end of its clause. This is one of a small set of conjunctions that do it, and forgetting is the most audible mistake at this level.

questions.stem: In „Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch“, why is it „dem Mann“?
options: The man is the indirect object, so it takes the dative
questions.explanation: Three cases at once: „ich“ nominative, „das Buch“ accusative, „dem Mann“ dative for the person receiving. German shows the roles through articles, which is why word order can move.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the small child is playing'?
questions.explanation: An adjective after „das“ takes -e in the nominative. German adjective endings depend on the article as well as the gender and case, which is the hardest table in the language and the reason to learn phrases whole.

questions.stem: Which article goes with a masculine singular noun in the nominative?
questions.explanation: „Der“ is masculine, „die“ feminine and „das“ neuter. „Den“ is the same masculine word once it becomes an object.

questions.stem: Which article goes with a feminine singular noun?
questions.explanation: „Die“ is feminine in the singular and also the plural for all three genders, which makes it the article you meet most often.

questions.stem: What is the indefinite article for a neuter noun?
questions.explanation: „Ein“ serves both masculine and neuter in the nominative; „eine“ is feminine. The endings only start to separate in the other cases.

questions.stem: Which noun ending is almost always feminine?
questions.explanation: Nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit and -schaft are feminine. Anything ending in -chen or -lein is neuter, however obviously female it is.

questions.stem: Why is „das Mädchen“ neuter?
options: The -chen ending makes any noun neuter
Nouns for young people are neuter
It is an exception with no rule
questions.explanation: The diminutive -chen overrides the meaning entirely, so a girl gets „das“. „Das Fräulein“ works the same way.

questions.stem: How is every German noun written?
questions.explanation: Every noun takes a capital, wherever it sits in the sentence. It is the single easiest German rule to apply and the easiest to forget.

questions.stem: Which is the correct plural of „der Mann“?
questions.explanation: German plurals are irregular and have to be learnt with the noun. This one adds an umlaut and -er, which is a common pattern for masculines.

questions.stem: Which is the correct plural of „die Frau“?
questions.explanation: Most feminine nouns add -n or -en. The article „die“ stays the same, so only the noun tells you it is plural.

questions.stem: Which position does the conjugated verb take in a German statement?
questions.explanation: Verb-second counts units of meaning, not words: „Morgen gehe ich“ puts a whole time phrase first and the verb still comes second.

questions.stem: Which sentence puts the verb in the right place?
questions.explanation: Something other than the subject starts the sentence, so the subject moves behind the verb. English would keep 'I' in front.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ihr ___ Deutsch“ (to learn)?
questions.explanation: „Ihr“ takes -t on a regular verb. It is the plural informal 'you', which English no longer distinguishes.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Sie ___ aus Australien“ (to come, formal you)?
questions.explanation: Formal „Sie“ always takes the same form as the plural, with a capital S wherever it appears.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Er ___ ein Buch“ (to read)?
questions.explanation: „Lesen“ changes its stem vowel in the du and er forms: du liest, er liest. Strong verbs do this and there is no way to predict which.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Du ___ nach Hause“ (to drive)?
questions.explanation: „Fahren“ takes an umlaut in the du and er forms. The ending is still -st for du.

questions.stem: What happens to a separable verb in a main clause?
options: The prefix goes to the end
The verb moves to the end
questions.explanation: „Aufstehen“ becomes „ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf“. The two halves split and the prefix waits at the end of the clause.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses the separable verb correctly?
options: Ich kaufe ein im Supermarkt heute
questions.explanation: „Einkaufen“ splits, with „ein“ at the very end of the clause. Everything else in the sentence sits between the two halves.

questions.stem: Which word makes a verb negative?
questions.explanation: „Nicht“ negates a verb or an adjective. „Kein“ goes in front of a noun and „nein“ is the answer to a question.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I have no time'?
questions.explanation: A noun that would otherwise take „ein“ or no article takes „kein“. Using „nicht“ here is the standard error.

questions.stem: What is the accusative form of „ein Hund“?
questions.explanation: Only the masculine changes in the accusative, taking -en. Feminine and neuter look exactly as they do in the nominative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I see the woman'?
questions.explanation: Feminine articles do not change between nominative and accusative, so „die“ stays. Only the masculine moves to „den“.

questions.stem: Which case does a direct object take?
questions.explanation: The thing having something done to it is accusative. The one doing it is nominative, and the one receiving it is dative.

questions.stem: Which case does an indirect object take?
questions.explanation: „Ich gebe dem Mann das Buch“ — the man receives, so he is dative; the book is given, so it is accusative.

questions.stem: What is the dative form of „die Frau“?
questions.explanation: Feminine „die“ becomes „der“ in the dative, which is exactly the form that looks masculine. The case is what tells you.

questions.stem: Which preposition always takes the dative?
questions.explanation: Mit, nach, aus, bei, seit, von and zu are always dative. Für, ohne, durch, gegen and um are always accusative.

questions.stem: Which preposition always takes the accusative?
questions.explanation: Durch, für, gegen, ohne and um take the accusative every time, whatever the sentence means.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going with my friend'?
questions.explanation: „Mit“ takes the dative, and a masculine possessive in the dative ends in -em. The preposition decides the ending, not the meaning.

questions.stem: Which possessive means 'your' for someone you call „du“?
questions.explanation: „Dein“ matches „du“. „Ihr“ is the formal 'your' and also 'her', which is why capitalisation matters in writing.

questions.stem: What does „Es gibt“ take after it?
questions.explanation: „Es gibt einen Park“ — the phrase means 'there is' but behaves as 'it gives', so what follows is a direct object.

questions.stem: Which question word means 'where'?
questions.explanation: „Wo“ is where, „wer“ is who, „was“ is what and „wann“ is when. „Wer“ and 'where' look alike and mean different things.

questions.stem: How do you form a yes/no question in German?
options: Add a question word at the end
questions.explanation: „Spielst du Fußball?“ — the finite verb leads. A question word instead pushes the verb back to second place.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly asks what someone is doing?
questions.explanation: The question word comes first and the verb second, so the subject follows the verb.

questions.stem: Where does the verb go after „weil“?
options: At the end of the clause
questions.explanation: Subordinating conjunctions send the verb to the end: „weil ich müde bin“. „Denn“ means the same thing and does not.

questions.stem: Which conjunction does not change the word order?
questions.explanation: Und, aber, oder, denn and sondern join clauses without touching the verb. Everything else on this list sends it to the end.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I know that he is coming'?
options: Ich weiß, dass er kommt nicht heute
questions.explanation: „Dass“ is subordinating, so the verb goes last and a comma separates the two clauses.

questions.stem: What order does German prefer for extra information?
questions.explanation: „Ich fahre morgen mit dem Bus in die Stadt“ — when, how, where. English tends to reverse the ends of that.

questions.stem: Which modal verb means 'to want'?
questions.explanation: Wollen is want, können is can, müssen is must and sollen is should. All of them send a second verb to the end as an infinitive.

questions.stem: Where does the second verb go after a modal?
options: At the end, as an infinitive
questions.explanation: „Ich muss Hausaufgaben machen“ — the modal takes second place and the infinitive waits at the end.

questions.stem: Which form completes „Ich ___ Deutsch sprechen“ (can)?
questions.explanation: Modals are irregular in the singular: ich kann, du kannst, er kann. The plural forms are regular.

questions.stem: Which word means 'but' after a negative, as in 'not X but Y'?
questions.explanation: „Nicht X, sondern Y“ corrects the first half. „Aber“ adds a contrast without contradicting.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am not going home'?
questions.explanation: „Nicht“ goes late but before the place phrase it is negating. Word order with „nicht“ is about what exactly is being denied.

questions.stem: What does „gern“ add to a sentence?
questions.explanation: „Ich spiele gern Fußball“ — I like playing football. German expresses liking an activity with an adverb rather than a verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I like reading'?
questions.explanation: „Gern“ follows the verb. „Mögen“ is used with nouns far more than with activities.

questions.stem: What is the German for 'I am fourteen years old'?
questions.explanation: German uses „sein“ for age, like English and unlike French. „Jahre alt“ is the usual full form.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'the book is on the table'?
options: Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch
Das Buch liegt auf den Tisch
Das Buch liegt auf der Tisch
Das Buch liegt auf das Tisch
questions.explanation: „Auf“ is a two-way preposition: position takes the dative, movement takes the accusative. Nothing is moving here.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am putting the book on the table'?
options: Ich lege das Buch auf der Tisch
Ich liege das Buch auf den Tisch
Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch
Ich lege das Buch auf dem Tisch
questions.explanation: Movement towards a place puts a two-way preposition into the accusative, so „dem“ becomes „den“.

questions.stem: What is the difference between „liegen“ and „legen“?
options: One describes lying, the other placing
One is formal and the other informal
One is present and the other past
They are spelling variants of one verb
questions.explanation: „Liegen“ is a position and takes the dative after a two-way preposition; „legen“ is an action and takes the accusative.

questions.stem: Which pronoun is the accusative of „er“?
questions.explanation: „Er“ becomes „ihn“ as an object and „ihm“ in the dative. Masculine pronouns change the most, exactly like the masculine article.

questions.stem: Which pronoun is the dative of „ich“?
questions.explanation: „Mich“ is the accusative and „mir“ the dative. „Gib mir das Buch“ — give the book to me.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'he helps me'?
questions.explanation: „Helfen“ takes the dative even though English treats 'me' as a direct object. A short list of verbs behave this way, including „danken“ and „folgen“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she is a teacher'?
options: Sie ist eine Lehrerin die arbeitet
questions.explanation: German drops the article in front of a job after „sein“, and the feminine form adds -in.

questions.stem: What does „Wie geht's?“ mean?
questions.explanation: Literally 'how goes it'. The reply is „Mir geht es gut“, with the person in the dative.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'there is a park here'?
questions.explanation: „Es gibt“ takes the accusative, so masculine „ein“ becomes „einen“.

questions.stem: Which word means 'also' or 'too'?
questions.explanation: „Auch“ means also. „Also“ is a false friend — in German it means 'so' or 'therefore'.

questions.stem: What does the false friend „bekommen“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Bekommen“ is to get or receive. 'To become' is „werden“, and confusing the two produces some memorable sentences.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I would like a coffee'?
options: Ich will einen Kaffee bitte haben
questions.explanation: „Möchte“ is the polite form and „Kaffee“ is masculine, so the accusative gives „einen“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'we are going by train'?
questions.explanation: Transport takes „mit“ plus the dative, and „fahren“ rather than „gehen“ — „gehen“ means on foot.

questions.stem: What is the plural of „das Kind“?
questions.explanation: „Kind“ adds -er. „Kindern“ is the dative plural, which adds a further -n on top of the plural form.

questions.stem: What happens to a plural noun in the dative?
questions.explanation: „Mit den Kindern“ — the dative plural adds -n unless the plural already ends in -n or -s, so „mit den Autos“ stays put.

questions.stem: Which word means 'and'?
questions.explanation: „Und“ is and, „aber“ is but, „oder“ is or and „denn“ is because. None of them move the verb.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'my sister is older than me'?
options: Meine Schwester ist mehr alt als ich
Meine Schwester ist älter als ich
Meine Schwester ist älter wie ich
Meine Schwester ist alter als ich
questions.explanation: Comparatives add -er and often an umlaut, and the comparison word is „als“ rather than „wie“.

questions.stem: What is the comparative of „groß“?
questions.explanation: „Groß“ takes an umlaut as well as -er. „Mehr“ is not used to build comparatives of short adjectives in German.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'it is raining'?
questions.explanation: Weather verbs take „es“ and nothing else. „Es schneit“ works the same way.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am cold'?
questions.explanation: German puts the person in the dative for how they feel. „Ich bin kalt“ says you are cold to the touch.

questions.stem: What does the prefix „un-“ do to a German adjective?
questions.explanation: „Freundlich“ becomes „unfreundlich“, exactly as in English. It is one of the few prefixes that behaves predictably.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'do you have a pen?' (informal)?
questions.explanation: Verb first for a yes/no question, and „Kuli“ is masculine so the accusative is „einen“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going to school'?
questions.explanation: Movement into a place puts „in“ into the accusative, so feminine „der“ becomes „die“.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am at school'?
options: Ich bin an der Schule heute
questions.explanation: No movement, so „in“ takes the dative and feminine „die“ becomes „der“.

questions.stem: What does „zu Hause“ mean?
questions.explanation: „Zu Hause“ is at home and „nach Hause“ is homewards. The pair has to be learnt together because English uses one word for both.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'I am going home'?
questions.explanation: Movement towards home takes „nach Hause“. Being there already takes „zu Hause“.

questions.stem: Which verb form completes „Wir ___ Fußball“ (to play)?
questions.explanation: „Wir“ takes the same form as the infinitive on every regular verb, which makes it the easiest ending in German.

questions.stem: Which sentence correctly says 'she has a brother and a sister'?
options: Sie hat ein Bruder und eine Schwester
Sie hat einen Bruder und einen Schwester
Sie hat eine Bruder und ein Schwester
Sie hat einen Bruder und eine Schwester
questions.explanation: Both nouns are objects, so masculine takes „einen“ and feminine keeps „eine“. Only the masculine changes.
